title: How to Hold a Pool Cue: A Beginner's Guide to a Light, Steady Grip
description: Squeezing your cue too hard? Learn where to hold a pool cue, how light your grip should be and how to fix common mistakes, in plain English.
body:
Picture this: you line up the perfect shot, squeeze the cue like you are trying to wring out a towel, and the cue ball sails off somewhere you never planned. Sound familiar? The fix is not more strength. It is a lighter, smarter grip. With the Mosconi Cup in Orlando drawing new fans to the table this weekend, here is a friendly guide to holding a pool cue the way the pros do.

Meet your two hands

Every pool shot uses two hands with two different jobs. Your bridge hand rests on the table and guides the front of the cue (see our guide to building a solid bridge and stance). Your grip hand is the back hand, usually your dominant one, and it swings the cue like a pendulum. This article is all about that back hand.

Where to hold the cue

Most coaches suggest holding the cue near the balance point, somewhere behind the middle of the stick, so the cue feels level and easy to control. When you are down on the shot, your forearm should hang roughly straight down from your elbow, with the cue meeting your hand at about a right angle. Sources differ on exact distances, so treat any number as a starting point. A simple test: set the cue on one finger until it balances, then slide your grip hand a few inches back from that spot and see how it feels.

Hold a little further back for long, smooth strokes, and a little further forward if you want a shorter, tighter stroke. Small changes are normal.

The bird trick: light grip pressure

This is where most beginners go wrong. A common coaching tip is to imagine you are holding a small bird: tight enough that it cannot fly away, gentle enough that you do not hurt it. Many teachers describe the right pressure as about a 2 or 3 on a scale of 1 to 10.

  • Too tight: your forearm tenses up, the stroke gets jerky, and the cue can twist at the last second.
  • Too loose: the cue wobbles or dangles, and your aim drifts.
  • Just right: the cue feels held, not squeezed, and your hand stays calm through the whole stroke.

Some well-known instructors prefer the word "cradle" over "grip." The idea is that the cue mostly rests in your fingers, with the thumb and first finger giving gentle support while the other fingers stay soft.

How to form the grip, step by step

  1. Stand relaxed with the cue pointing at the cue ball and your elbow hanging under your shoulder.
  2. Open your hand and lay the cue across your fingers, not deep in your palm.
  3. Close your thumb and first finger softly around the cue, like a loose ring.
  4. Let the remaining fingers wrap around lightly, with no white knuckles.
  5. Keep your wrist straight and neutral, with no sharp curl up or down.
  6. Take a few slow practice strokes and check that the cue travels in a straight line.

Keep it steady during the stroke

Once you settle into a grip, keep it the same from the first practice swing through the follow-through. Opening and closing your hand mid-stroke changes the cue's path, and that is a common cause of misses. Think of your elbow as a hinge: your upper arm stays quiet while your forearm swings smoothly back and forward. If you are working on a repeatable routine, our guide to a pre-shot routine pairs nicely with a calm grip.

Common grip mistakes

  • The death grip: squeezing the cue hard. Fix it by loosening each finger until the cue just stays in place.
  • Gripping too far forward or back: if the cue tips up or the butt hits your body, slide your hand a few inches.
  • A wandering wrist: twisting or flipping the wrist on the follow-through. Try a slow, straight, smooth finish.
  • Clamping the bridge hand too: the front hand should also use light pressure, just enough to hold the cue steady.

A quick practice drill

Place the cue ball in the middle of the table and shoot it straight to the end rail and back, aiming to have it return to the same spot. Do ten shots with a light grip and ten with a tight one, and notice which feels smoother and straighter. For more solo ideas, try our 5 solo pool drills.

Watching the pros

The 2026 Mosconi Cup is on at the Caribe Royale Resort in Orlando, Florida, from November 27 to 30, with ESPN+ carrying coverage and ESPN2 on Sunday, according to ESPN's schedule. Next time you watch, look at the back hands. You will see relaxed fingers and a smooth, quiet swing, even under big pressure. You can follow the whole event on our Mosconi Cup hub, or find a local event on the tournaments page.

The takeaway

A great grip is mostly about doing less. Hold the cue lightly, keep your wrist calm and repeat the same hand position every shot. Give it a week of easy practice and you may be surprised how much straighter the cue ball travels.
